text: Welcome to Bench Tech! You've just opened a little electronics repair shop. This walkthrough fixes your first job with you , a desk lamp that will not turn on , one step at a time, then shows you around the office. Takes about 10 minutes. You can skip it now or at any point, and replay it later from the Help button. Click Start the tutorial.

Welcome to your shop office. This is the office: customers wait here, and so do your supplies, orders and money. Robin T has brought in a broken lamp. In the list of customers waiting, each job shows the customer, the device, the price, and a Start button. Click Start beside Robin T.

Read the ticket, then click Next. The repair ticket is the panel at the top left. It shows the customer, the quote and what they noticed. Under it are buttons for the case, for returning the job, for calling the customer, and for the service sheet. The ticket says what the customer noticed: completely dead. Always start with the symptom. Stuck later? Need a nudge? on the ticket gives a hint, and the Service sheet shows the board's blocks and test points.

Click Customer adapter. The Power panel is on the right, under the multimeter. Its buttons choose what powers the board: off, the customer's adapter, or your own bench power supply. The customer's own adapter powers the lamp. Watch the status lines under the buttons: nothing lights up. Now let's find out why.

Click test point 1 with the red probe. Test points are the small round pads on the board. This one is flashing, with a number on it. The multimeter panel at the top right shows the reading, and its Red and Black boxes show where each probe is. The multimeter is set to volts, and we have clipped its black probe to ground , test point 5, for you. The Black ground button does that any time. The red probe goes on the raw input, where the adapter's power arrives.

Click test point 2. Test point 2 is flashing on the board, a little further along from the first. The multimeter panel at the top right shows the reading and where each probe sits. test point 1 reads about 12 V: power is getting into the board. test point 2 is the 12 V rail a little further along, after the protection parts.

Click Off. The Off button is the first button in the Power panel on the right. test point 2 reads 0 V! Power gets in at test point 1 but is lost before test point 2. The only part between them is the fuse, F 1, so let's test it. Resistance, continuity and diode tests only make sense with the power off.

Click the continuity mode on the multimeter. The multimeter is the panel at the top right. Its row of four buttons chooses what it measures: volts, resistance, continuity, which beeps, and a diode test. In continuity mode the meter beeps when the two probes are connected through almost nothing: perfect for checking a fuse.

First, Left-click one end of F 1 , red probe. Then, Right-click the other end of F 1 , black probe. The Red and Black boxes in the multimeter panel show where each probe is. A left-click puts the red probe on a pad, and a right-click puts the black one. A good fuse beeps and reads close to 0 ohms.

First, Choose Soldering , key 3, later: click Rework at the microscope. Then, Click the fuse F 1 on the board. The toolbar along the bottom chooses what your mouse does: multimeter, inspect, soldering and more. Click a part with Soldering and a card about it opens on the left, with a Rework at the microscope button. No beep, and the meter reads O L, an open circuit: the fuse has blown. Found it! The part card that opens on the left has the button that takes you to the microscope.

Click Flux , or press 3. You are now at the microscope. The big picture on the left is a close-up of the fuse and its pads. The tool buttons are the grid at the top right: Iron, Wick, Flux, Tweezers, Hot air, Liquid, Brush and Wipe, each with its keyboard number. Welcome to the microscope. The yellow hint box on the right always suggests the next move. First, flux: it lets the heat flow and the old solder run.

Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. Your mouse is the tool in the microscope picture on the left. A yellow ring marks each pad that still needs flux. Flux on both ends of the fuse helps the heat flow and the old solder run.
Click Wick , or press 2. The Wick is the second button in the tool grid at the top right. The wick is a copper braid: heated, it soaks the molten solder up off the pad.

Hold the wick on each marked joint until the solder is gone. The Joints panel lower on the right lists each pad: its solder bar, its temperature, and its pad heat bar, which fills as the pad gets too hot. Warning. Heat kills pads. A pad that stays molten for about ten seconds, or gets far above 320 degrees, burns and lifts off the board, and the repair is ruined. Work in short bursts, watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Press and hold on a joint: the iron heats through the braid and the solder runs into it. The pad should end up bare copper. If the wick end turns silver, cut it off with C; if the flux is gone, add more.
Click Tweezers , or press 4. The Tweezers are the fourth button in the tool grid at the top right. The tweezers pick parts up and set them down.

Click the fuse to pick it up with the tweezers. The fuse is the part in the middle of the microscope picture. When you click it, the tweezers pick it up and it follows your mouse. The solder is off, so nothing holds the fuse down any more.
Press Delete on your keyboard to bin the fuse in the tweezers. The Delete key is on your keyboard. Whatever the tweezers are holding gets thrown away. The blown fuse is no use to anyone any more.

Click New beside Fuse 1A fast in the Parts tray. The Parts tray is the list on the right, below the tool settings. Each row is a part you can use, with a New button that takes one from your stock. It comes out of your stock and lands in the tweezers.

Click the empty footprint to set the fuse down on the pads. The empty outline in the middle of the microscope picture is the fuse's footprint, with a pad at each end. The new fuse follows your mouse until you click. It only counts if it sits on both pads.
Click Flux , or press 3. The Flux button is the third button in the tool grid at the top right. Flux again, so the solder flows into the new joints.

Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. A yellow ring marks each pad that still needs flux, in the microscope picture on the left. Fresh flux on both pads helps the new solder flow.

Click Iron , or press 1. The Iron is the first button in the tool grid at the top right. Its temperature slider is at the top of the window. The iron heats the pad, and the solder wire melts into the joint.

Look at the Joints section on the right, then click Got it. The Joints section is lower down in the right-hand panel. It has one row for each pad, with its solder bar, its heat bar and its temperature. The panel has been scrolled to Joints. Each pad shows its solder bar , about half full = a good joint, no blob, its temperature, and a Pad heat bar: if that one fills, the pad burns off the board.

Press and hold the mouse button on the marked pad until the readout says MOLTEN. In the Joints panel, the temperature beside each pad rises while you heat it, and it says MOLTEN once the solder has melted. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Hold the iron's tip on the pad , hover it to read its temperature. Solder melts at about 220 degrees, so MOLTEN appears long before the pad is in danger. Keep the pad under about 320 degrees.

Keep the iron on the pad , still MOLTEN, and hold Space for 1 to 2 seconds. The solder bar in the Joints panel fills as solder goes onto the pad. The mark in the middle of the bar is the half-way line. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Holding Space feeds solder wire into the molten joint. In the Joints panel the solder bar should reach about half , 50 percent,: a solid joint without a blob. Then let go and lift the iron.

Press and hold the mouse button on the marked pad until the readout says MOLTEN. In the Joints panel, the second row is this pad. Its temperature rises while you heat it. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Hold the iron's tip on the pad , hover it to read its temperature. Solder melts at about 220 degrees, so MOLTEN appears long before the pad is in danger. Keep the pad under about 320 degrees.

Keep the iron on the pad , still MOLTEN, and hold Space for 1 to 2 seconds. The solder bar for this pad is in the Joints panel. The mark in the middle of the bar is the half-way line. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Holding Space feeds solder wire into the molten joint. In the Joints panel the solder bar should reach about half , 50 percent,: a solid joint without a blob. Then let go and lift the iron.

Click Flux , or press 3. The Flux button is the third button in the tool grid at the top right. A hot-air reflow melts both joints together so the solder flows evenly and the fuse pulls itself straight. It needs fresh flux first.

Click or hold on every marked pad , clicking again adds more flux. A yellow ring marks each pad that still needs flux, in the microscope picture on the left. Fresh flux lets the solder flow evenly during the reflow.

Click Hot air , or press 5. The Hot air button is the fifth button in the tool grid at the top right. Its temperature slider is at the top of the window. Hot air heats the whole part evenly, with no tip touching the pads.

Hold the mouse button and sweep back and forth over both joints until they read 300 to 320 degrees, then let go. The dashed circle around your mouse is the area the hot air nozzle heats. The temperature of each pad shows in the Joints panel on the right. Watch the pad heat bar, and let go before it fills. Keep the nozzle moving over both joints at the same time. The flux bubbles as it heats. Hover a pad for its temperature. When both are about 300 to 320 degrees, stop: any longer and the pads start to burn.

Click Liquid , or press 6. The Liquid button is the sixth button in the tool grid at the top right. The flux has done its job and what is left is sticky. Let go of the hot air first, then pick the Liquid tool to clean it off.

Make sure Cleaning liquid says Isopropyl alcohol , I P A, then click Next. The Cleaning liquid selector is in the tool settings on the right, under the tool grid. The Cleaning liquid selector decides what the Liquid tool applies. For flux, use I P A , isopropyl alcohol.

Hold the Liquid tool on each marked joint until the flux dissolves into the I P A. The wet look on a pad shows the liquid, and it turns cloudy where flux has dissolved into it. Keep it wet until the flux melts into the I P A: the liquid turns cloudy and yellowish.
Click Brush , or press 7. The Brush is the seventh button in the tool grid at the top right. The brush loosens the dissolved flux. Only scrub while the pad is wet.

Scrub back and forth over each marked joint until the flux ovals disappear. Move the brush back and forth over a pad in the microscope picture. The faint flux ovals around the pads fade as it loosens the flux. If the I P A dries before you finish, pick the Liquid tool and add a little more.

Click Wipe , or press 8. The Wipe is the eighth and last button in the tool grid at the top right. The wipe lifts the dissolved flux away. One side has already dried, leaving white residue marks: that is what happens when I P A evaporates before you wipe.
Drag the wipe across the joint that is still wet. Drag the wipe over a pad in the microscope picture to lift the wet liquid and flux away. Save the side that is still wet first.
Click Liquid , or press 6. The Liquid button is the sixth button in the tool grid at the top right. The white marks are dried flux. Do not scrape them: dissolve them again with I P A.

Hold the Liquid tool on the marked residue until it turns liquid again. White marks around a pad are dried flux. Keep the liquid on them in the microscope picture until they turn wet and cloudy again. When the white residue goes cloudy and wet, it can be wiped.
Click Wipe , or press 8. The Wipe is the eighth and last button in the tool grid at the top right. Now wipe it away, quickly, before it dries again.
Drag the wipe over the marked joints until they are clean. Drag the wipe over the pads in the microscope picture until no marks are left. The pads should end up clean and shiny.

Click Done to put the board back on the bench. The Done button is green and sits at the top right of the microscope window, next to Undo all, which puts the board back exactly as it was. Clean, shiny joints. Messed up , a lifted pad, a blob, a crooked fuse? Click Undo all instead: the board goes back exactly as it was when you sat down, and you can try again.

Click Undo all, then confirm. The Undo all button is at the top right of the microscope window, next to Done. Too much heat for too long: a copper pad burned and peeled off the board. A fuse soldered to it would not connect, and the lamp would stay dead. No harm done in the tutorial. The board goes back exactly as it was when you sat down, and you can try again. This time, work in short bursts and watch the Pad heat bar.
Click Customer adapter. The Power panel is on the right, under the multimeter. Customer adapter plugs the customer's own charger back in. Back on the bench. Time to test it the way the customer will.

Press and hold the lamp button , or hold Space. The lamp button is in the Power panel, below the status lines. It works like the switch on the lamp. You can also hold the space bar. The lamp should light up. If it doesn't, re-check your joints at the microscope.

Click Case: open. The Case button is on the repair ticket at the top left. It says whether the lamp's case is open or closed. It lights up, so the fuse is fixed! The lamp is still out of its case, so let's put it back together.

Click Close it up for me. This is the case workbench. Close it up for me, on the right, puts the case back together for you. This is the teardown bench, where you take cases apart and put them back together, screw by screw.
Click Done. The Done button is at the top right of the case window. All screwed back together.
Click Return to customer. Return to customer is the green button on the repair ticket at the top left. The lamp is fixed and closed up. Time to hand it back.

Click Return to Robin T. A window asks you to confirm. The button with the customer's name hands the lamp back. Robin tests it at home. Good work gets paid and builds your reputation; sloppy joints can come back later as free warranty repairs.

That's the job! You found the fault, swapped the fuse like a pro and got paid. Next, a quick tour of the office, where you run the business side of the shop. That is the end of the repair. The shop office, with everything else you can do, comes next. Click Tour the office.

The Overview tab is your shop at a glance: today's alerts , low supplies, rent due, deliveries on the way, profit and loss for today and the week, and the ledger of every payment in and out. The row of tabs across the top of the office window switches between its pages. The End day button is in the bar above the tabs. Click Next to see the Work tab.

The Work tab lists the customers waiting and the devices you own , your projects. Click Start to put one on the bench. Customers don't wait forever , after about three days they collect their device unrepaired. The Work tab is the second tab in the row across the top of the office. Click Next to see Supplies and parts.

On Supplies & parts you buy what the microscope uses up: solder, flux, wick, I P A, brushes and wipes. Run out and that tool stops working. To buy: click + next to a pack to add it to the Order basket. Supplies and parts is the third tab. The Consumables list is on the left, with a plus and minus button beside each pack, and the Order basket is on the right. Click Next to see the parts list.

Further down is Components in stock: every fuse, resistor, capacitor and chip you have, and what they cost. Use + to add parts to the basket too. In the Order basket, pick a delivery speed and click Place order , it arrives on a later morning. Cheap parts can also be rush-bought one at a time from the microscope's parts tray; expensive chips are special order. The Components in stock list is further down the same page. Each row has the part, how many you have, its price, and plus and minus buttons. Click Next to see the Store-room.

The Store-room holds donor boards: repairs you gave up on and parts-only devices you bought. Pull parts off them , retimers, screens, programmed chips , when a job needs one and nobody sells it new. The Store-room is the fourth tab in the row across the top of the office. Click Next to see Equipment.

Equipment sells new capabilities: an ESR meter, an oscilloscope, a thermal camera, microscope upgrades, test consoles for cartridges, and better iron tips and hot-air nozzles. Choose tips and nozzles in the microscope's kit selectors. Equipment is the fifth tab. Each card shows a tool, its price and a Buy button. Click Next to see the Marketplace.

The Marketplace sells broken devices. Buy one with Buy for $…: a normal listing goes to Work Your projects to repair and sell on for profit; a parts only listing goes to the store-room as a donor to stockpile parts. Need one exact chip? Search online for a donor of that device at the top. The Marketplace is the sixth tab. Each card is a listing with its price and a Buy button, and the search box for donor devices is at the top of the page. Click Next to see Advertising.

Advertising brings in more customers each day, and people who find you through ads accept slightly higher quotes. It's billed every night, so start small. Advertising is the seventh and last tab. Each card is a level of advertising with its daily cost and a Choose button. Click Next to see what End day does.

When you're done for the day, click End day. Tonight's bills get paid , electricity, rent every 7 days, advertising, orders arrive, and new customers come in the next morning. The End day button is the green button at the top right of the office window. Click Next to learn about starting a new career.

Want a fresh start? The Career card on the Overview tab has ⟲ Start a new career: back to day 1 with a new shop, starting cash and a starter pack of parts. It wipes the current save. The Career card is on the Overview tab, at the bottom of the page. Its button starts a brand new career. Click Next to find out how to replay this tutorial.

Forgot something? Click the Help button at the top right any time , it explains the controls and has Play the tutorial to run this walkthrough again. That's everything. Good luck with the shop! The Help button is at the top right of the screen, next to the View button. Inside it is a Play the tutorial button. Click Finish to start playing.
